title: The Old World, in depth
lead: What the Certified exam adds for Europe’s classic regions, from Bordeaux to Greece: classifications, aging laws, more appellations, iconic producers and pairings. Champagne in depth is in chapter six.

intro.title: WHAT CERTIFIED ADDS
intro.text: Level 1 placed each region and its grapes on the map. Certified adds the rules, the names and the table.

sections.name: Bordeaux

lines.label: More places
lines.text: Pessac-Léognan and Barsac in Graves; Lalande-de-Pomerol and Montagne-Saint-Émilion beside the Right Bank stars.

lines.label: At the table
lines.text: Decant young Bordeaux for air and old Bordeaux for its sediment. Bold reds suit beef and lamb; sweet Sauternes suits dessert and foie gras.

know: Château d’Yquem is the only Premier Cru Supérieur of Sauternes and Barsac.
The Graves classification ranks 14 Pessac-Léognan châteaux for red, white or both.
Saint-Émilion’s ranking has three tiers and is revised every ten years; Pomerol has none.
Crus Bourgeois du Médoc has three levels, up to Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel.
Noble rot helps Sauternes; black and grey rot and spring frost hurt a vintage.

sections.name: Burgundy and Beaujolais

lines.label: Chablis
lines.text: Petit Chablis grows on harder Portlandian limestone; Chablis and its crus on Kimmeridgian limestone and marl. Spring frost is the classic danger.

lines.label: In the cellar
lines.text: The Court adds bâtonnage, cold soak, whole-cluster fermentation, the pièce barrel and chaptalization, and how oak use changes by level.

know: Chablis has seven Grands Crus, including Les Clos, Valmur and Vaudésir.
Bouzeron is the only village appellation made only from Aligoté.
Côte Chalonnaise villages: Bouzeron, Rully, Mercurey, Givry, Montagny.
Morgon is the largest Beaujolais cru; Côte du Py is its famous lieu-dit.
Monks and the Napoleonic inheritance code shaped the crus and split up vineyards.

sections.name: The Loire and Alsace

lines.label: Loire
lines.text: Tuffeau under Vouvray, plus silex and Kimmeridgian clay. Humidity from the Layon River brings botrytis to Quarts de Chaume and Bonnezeaux.

lines.label: Alsace
lines.text: Bas-Rhin, to the north, is lower and less sheltered by the Vosges. Haut-Rhin, to the south, is higher and more sheltered, with many of the best sites.

know: Chenin label words: Sec, Demi-Sec and Moelleux; Vouvray can also be Pétillant.
Domaine Huet and Nicolas Joly are the Loire producers the Court names.
Alsace ages wine in big neutral casks called foudres, with little new oak.
Every Alsace AOP wine goes in the traditional Flûte d’Alsace bottle.
Alsace names to know: Trimbach, Weinbach, Zind-Humbrecht, Hugel, Marcel Deiss.

lines.label: Rhône
lines.text: Lyon lies to the north and Avignon is the south’s main city; Montélimar is the unofficial dividing line. North: decomposed granite and schist. South: galets, alluvium and limestone.

lines.label: South of France
lines.text: Provence, Languedoc-Roussillon, the Southwest and the Dordogne each have their own grapes. The Court asks you to match each AOP to its grape and style.

know: Côte-Rôtie is the only northern red cru to plant Viognier alongside Syrah.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape may use 18 grape varieties; its bottles can carry the papal crest.
Bandol is at least 50% Mourvèdre; Côtes de Provence is mostly dry rosé.
Cahors is Côt (Malbec), Madiran is Tannat, Jurançon is Gros and Petit Manseng.
Banyuls and Muscat de Rivesaltes are Vins Doux Naturels, made by mutage.

lines.label: Piedmont
lines.text: Barolo ages 38 months (18 in oak); Barbaresco 26 months (9 in oak). Riserva takes five years for Barolo and four for Barbaresco.

lines.text: Valtellina calls it Chiavennasca; Gattinara and Ghemme call it Spanna.

Alta Langa DOCG is metodo classico, at least 90% Pinot Noir and/or Chardonnay.
Franciacorta Satèn is Brut only, max 5 atmospheres, Chardonnay with up to 50% Pinot Bianco.
Lambrusco subzones: Sorbara, Grasparossa di Castelvetro, Salamino di Santa Croce.
Friuli is known for orange and natural wines; Gravner is the name to know.

sections.name: Tuscany, the South and the islands

lines.label: Montalcino
lines.text: Clay and marine sediments lie low; galestro sits higher up. Brunello is Sangiovese with 2 years in oak and 4 months in bottle.

lines.label: The south
lines.text: Match each DOCG to its region: Campania’s Taurasi, Greco di Tufo and Fiano di Avellino; Umbria’s Sagrantino di Montefalco; Sicily’s Cerasuolo di Vittoria.

know: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese, called Prugnolo Gentile there.
Gran Selezione is Chianti Classico’s top tier: 90% Sangiovese, estate grapes, 30 months.
Decant young Brunello, Taurasi and Sagrantino di Montefalco.
Etna DOC: white from Carricante, red from Nerello Mascalese, on volcanic soil.
Marsala is Sicily’s fortified wine: Secco, Semi-Secco or Dolce.

sections.name: Spain and Portugal

lines.label: Rioja
lines.text: Alta is continental, Alavesa the coolest and wettest, Oriental Mediterranean. Gran Reserva is usually made only in the best vintages.

lines.label: Portugal
lines.text: The Douro has three subregions: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior. Dão, Bairrada and Alentejo are DOPs to know.

know: Rioja and Ribera tinto: Crianza 2 years (1 in oak), Reserva 3 (1), Gran Reserva 5 (2).
Cava de Guarda needs 9 months on the lees; Reserva needs 18.
Tempranillo is Tinta del País in Ribera del Duero and Tinta de Toro in Toro.
Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra make Mencía; Valdeorras makes Godello.
Vino de Pago began in 2003: producer appellations, 20 of them by 2022.

sections.name: Germany and Austria

lines.label: Germany
lines.text: Beyond the Mosel and Rheingau: Nahe, Franken, Baden, Mittelrhein and Ahr. The VDP ranks vineyards on a Burgundy model.

lines.label: Austria
lines.text: Kremstal and Kamptal DACs make dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling. The Wachau grades dry wines Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd.

know: Franken uses the flat, round Bocksbeutel bottle and is known for Silvaner.
The Ahr, north of the 50th parallel, makes some of Germany’s best Spätburgunder.
Baden is Germany’s warmest growing area.
The 1971 wine law made ripeness at harvest the measure of quality.
The Banderole is Austria’s capsule for Qualitätswein and above.

sections.name: Hungary and Greece

lines.label: Tokaji
lines.text: Humidity from the Bodrog River helps noble rot form. Furmint and Hárslevelű shrivel into aszú berries for the sweet wine.

lines.label: Greece
lines.text: Three PDOs to know: Santorini (Assyrtiko), Naoussa (Xinomavro) and Nemea (Agiorgitiko).

know: Since 2013, Tokaji Aszú needs at least 120 g/L of sugar and 18 months in cask.
Eszencia is made entirely from aszú berries.
Tokaji usually comes in 500 ml bottles.
Santorini vines are trained into low baskets (kouloura) against the wind.
Naoussa is 100% Xinomavro; Nemea is 100% Agiorgitiko.

facts.fact: CMS Certified learning outcomes for the Old World subjects add classification systems, aging requirements and label laws, more appellations and crus, iconic producers, and recommending and selling food pairings to a guest.
CMS Introductory learning outcomes for the same subjects focus on locating regions on a map and connecting grape varieties, climate and main appellations.
The Certified curriculum includes and builds from the Introductory curriculum; Certified-only subjects include South France, Spain Other DOs and Greece.
CMS Certified rows include service of beverage items such as glassware (Burgundy, Rhône) and decanting (Bordeaux, Brunello, Taurasi, Sagrantino).

Bordeaux Certified column: Graves area adds Barsac AOP; Right Bank adds Lalande-de-Pomerol AOP and Montagne-St-Émilion AOP (alongside Pessac-Léognan, Sauternes, Pomerol, St-Émilion from the Intro column).
Bordeaux, Left Bank Cabernet Sauvignon on gravel and Right Bank Merlot on clay/limestone (Level 1 recap).

1855 has 88 classified growths: reds in five levels (Premier to Cinquième Cru) - 60 Médoc estates plus Château Haut-Brion in Graves (Pessac); sweet whites in three levels (Premier Cru Supérieur, Premier Cru, Second Cru) - 27 châteaux in Sauternes and Barsac.

Conseil des Grands Crus Classés en 1855 list, Seconds Crus include: Rauzan-Ségla (Margaux), Rauzan-Gassies (Margaux), Léoville-Poyferré (Saint-Julien), Léoville Barton (Saint-Julien), Durfort-Vivens (Margaux), Gruaud Larose (Saint-Julien), Lascombes (Margaux), Brane-Cantenac (Margaux), Pichon Baron (Pauillac), Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande (Pauillac), Ducru-Beaucaillou (Saint-Julien), Cos d'Estournel (Saint-Estèphe), Montrose (Saint-Estèphe).
CMS Certified column: know the First Growths and the Second Growths (14), each with château and commune.
Sauternes and Barsac 1855: Château d'Yquem (Sauternes) is the single Premier Cru Supérieur; Premiers Crus include Climens and Coutet (Barsac), Suduiraut and Rieussec (Sauternes).
Graves classification: 14 châteaux, all in Pessac-Léognan, classified for red, white or both; first list 1953, one change 1959; Haut-Brion is in both Graves and 1855 lists.
Saint-Émilion classification: first in 1955, revised every ten years. Three levels: Premiers Grands Crus Classés 'A', Premiers Grands Crus Classés, Grands Crus Classés.
2022 Premiers Grands Crus Classés 'A': Château Figeac and Château Pavie.
Crus Bourgeois du Médoc: three levels (Cru Bourgeois, Cru Bourgeois Supérieur, Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel); revised every five years since 2020.
CMS Certified column: Cru Bourgeois created in the 1930s with three levels; Pomerol has no classification.

CMS Certified column: Pomerol top producers include Château Pétrus, Château Lafleur, Le Pin, Clos l'Église; St-Émilion top producers: Angélus, Ausone, Cheval-Blanc, Pavie, Figeac; Graves top producer Haut-Brion; Sauternes top producer d'Yquem.

CMS Certified column (Bordeaux grape growing): humidity from water and spring rain brings mold and rot - black and grey rot (bad), noble rot (good for sweet wines); springtime frosts; Bordeaux mixture.

CMS Certified column (Bordeaux): know top vintages of the last 15 years; history includes the marriage of Eleanor of Aquitaine, Dutch draining of the Gironde estuary and the slave trade port; today the largest region of AOP wine production in France.
CMS Certified column (Bordeaux service): decant young Bordeaux for aeration and aged Bordeaux for sediment; know service temperatures.
CMS Certified column (Bordeaux pairing): bold red wines with beef and lamb; rich sweet wines with dessert and foie gras.
Chablis Grand Cru has seven Climats: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur, Vaudésir.
Chablis soils: Kimmeridgian limestone and marl (Chablis, Premier Cru, Grand Cru on the hillsides); harder Portlandian limestone mainly for Petit Chablis on higher slopes and plateau.
Premier Cru labels show the commune then the Climat, e.g. 'Chablis Premier Cru, Montée de Tonnerre'.

CMS Certified column (Burgundy): Chablis AOP vs Petit Chablis AOP; know all seven Chablis Grands Crus; frost hazard in Chablis; know all Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune villages and their Grands Crus; Côte de Nuits-Villages AOP and Côte de Beaune-Villages AOP; identify the 10 Beaujolais Crus; Côte du Py lieu-dit in Morgon.
Burgundy hierarchy: Régionale, Village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru (Level 1 recap); 33 Grand Cru appellations.

Côte de Nuits Grands Crus listed by BIVB include Chambertin, Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, Clos de la Roche, Clos de Tart, Clos de Vougeot, Échezeaux, Richebourg, Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Musigny, Bonnes Mares. It is the centre of the region's Grands Crus, mainly red Pinot Noir.

Côte de Beaune: around Beaune mainly Pinot Noir (Volnay, Pommard); from Meursault south, Chardonnay dominates. Grands Crus: Corton, Corton-Charlemagne, Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet, Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet.
Côte Chalonnaise Village appellations: Bouzeron, Givry, Mercurey, Montagny, Rully. Thought to be the cradle of Crémant de Bourgogne.
Bouzeron is the only Village appellation made exclusively from Aligoté.
CMS Certified column (Burgundy): Mâcon - Pouilly-Fuissé AOP has Premier Cru designated vineyards; Côte Chalonnaise: Bouzeron AOP white from 100% Aligoté, Rully, Mercurey, Givry, Montagny.
The 10 Beaujolais crus: Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Côte de Brouilly, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié, Saint-Amour.
Morgon is the largest Beaujolais cru; its famous Côte du Py is decomposed shale.

CMS Certified column (Burgundy winemaking): bâtonnage; cold soak; stem inclusion, whole-cluster fermentation, semi-carbonic maceration; pièce barrel size; chaptalization; oak use varies by level in Chablis, Mâconnais and Beaujolais.

CMS Certified column (Burgundy producers): distinguish négociants from domaines. Chablis: Dauvissat, Raveneau. Côte d'Or: DRC, Leroy, Coche-Dury, Domaine Leflaive, Roulot. Larger négociants: Louis Jadot, Louis Latour, Albert Bichot, Bouchard Père et Fils/William Fèvre, Drouhin, Faiveley.

CMS Certified column (Burgundy history): the monastic influence and the Napoleonic Code of inheritance shaped classification, fragmentation of vineyards and vineyard ownership. Non-wine production: Marc de Bourgogne. Label terms: négociant, domaine, clos, monopole, vieilles vignes; lieu-dit.
CMS Certified column (Burgundy service/pairing): proper glassware for white and red Burgundy; oak, acid and tannin levels matter for pairing; classic Burgundian dishes.
Chaptalization: adding sugar to unfermented grape must to increase alcohol after fermentation; used when grapes do not reach enough sugar ripeness.
CMS Certified column (Loire): soils - tuffeau in Vouvray; silex; Kimmeridgian clay. Layon River. Botrytis in Bonnezeaux and Quarts-de-Chaume from river humidity.

CMS Certified column (Loire): sparkling wines Vouvray Pétillant and Crémant de Loire; label terms sur lie, sec, demi-sec, moelleux; producers Domaine Huet and Nicolas Joly; pair the different sweetness levels of Chenin Blanc; classic pairings with Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé.
Loire sweet terms: moelleux = 10-45 g/L residual sugar; liquoreux = over 45 g/L. (Translated from French.)
Loire sparkling wines use the traditional method; minimum 9 months on laths for Crémant de Loire and 12 months for Vouvray.

CMS Certified column (Alsace): Bas-Rhin lies to the north, lower average elevation, less protected by the Vosges; Haut-Rhin lies to the south, higher, more protected; many of the best regarded vineyard sites are in the Haut-Rhin.

CMS Certified column (Alsace): very diverse soils (marl, limestone, gneiss, schist, sandstone, granite, clay, volcanic); large neutral casks called foudres, little to no new oak; extra white grapes Pinot Blanc, Silvaner, Chardonnay, Auxerrois; Alsace AOP wines must be bottled in the 'Vin du Rhin' / 'Flûte d'Alsace' bottle.
CMS Certified column (Alsace Grands Crus): examples Schlossberg, Brand, Goldert, Hengst; one Grand Cru uses Sylvaner, two allow blending, two allow red wine; Pinot Noir added as of the 2022 vintage.
Alsace Grand Cru grapes: Riesling, Muscat, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer; Sylvaner allowed in Zotzenberg; co-planting practised in Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf.
Edelzwicker and Gentil are Alsace blends.

CMS Certified column (Alsace): producers Trimbach, Domaine Weinbach, Marcel Deiss, Hugel et Fils, Pierre Sparr, Zind-Humbrecht; history of French and German rule; pairings choucroute, flammkuchen (tarte flambée), baeckeoffe, cured meats; Crémant d'Alsace is a cost-effective traditional method sparkling wine.

CMS Certified column (Rhône): Lyon to the north; Montélimar the unofficial dividing line; Avignon the main city of the south. North: steep hills, the river reflects light and concentrates the Mistral. South: rolling hills.
CMS Certified column (Rhône soils): Northern Rhône decomposed granite and schist; Southern Rhône galets, alluvial, limestone. Modern southern plantings are often trellised.

CMS Certified column (Rhône): co-fermented wines in the north; blended wines in the south; minimum abv in Châteauneuf-du-Pape and minimum Grenache rules in Southern Rhône AOPs; producers Chave, Chapoutier, Guigal, Beaucastel, Rayas; papal crest on bottles; glassware for Syrah and Grenache; pair with meaty dishes with herbs, bacon, peppercorn; white Rhône as a Chardonnay alternative.
Côte-Rôtie is the only red cru in the Northern Côtes du Rhône to plant Viognier alongside Syrah.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape lists 18 associated grape varieties, including Grenache Noir, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Counoise, Clairette and Roussanne.
Vins Doux Naturels such as Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau are made by mutage (adding alcohol to stop fermentation).

CMS Certified column (South France): Provence - nearly 90% dry rosé production; grapes Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre; Côtes de Provence AOP dry rosé dominant; Bandol AOP Mourvèdre min 50% with Grenache and Cinsault, dry red dominant.

CMS Certified column (South France): Languedoc-Roussillon - Limoux AOP (Mauzac, Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay; dry whites); Crémant de Limoux (traditional method white and rosé); Fitou AOP (Grenache, Carignan, Syrah, Mourvèdre; dry reds); Banyuls AOP/Banyuls Grand Cru (Grenache; VDN); Muscat de Rivesaltes (Muscat; VDN); large amount of IGP wine, Pays d'Oc IGP; mutage stops fermentation with neutral grape spirit.

CMS Certified column (South France): Southwest - Cahors AOP Côt (Malbec)-dominant, dry reds only; Madiran AOP Tannat-dominant, dry reds only; Jurançon AOP Gros and Petit Manseng, sec (dry) and off-dry whites. Dordogne - Bergerac AOP (Bordeaux grapes; white, red and rosé); Monbazillac AOP botrytis-affected sweet wines (Muscadelle, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon).

CMS Certified column (South France): producers Bandol - Domaine Tempier, Château de Pibarnon, Château Pradeaux; Banyuls - Chapoutier, Domaine du Mas Blanc. Provence: birthplace of wine in France, wine since 600 BCE. Pairings: dry rosé with shellfish, fish, bouillabaisse; Bandol with beef, lamb; Banyuls with chocolate, nuts, coffee; Cahors and Madiran with duck breast, lamb, cassoulet.
CMS Certified column (Piedmont): Barolo 38 months total aging with a min of 18 months in oak; Barbaresco 26 months total with min 9 months in oak.
Barolo: only after five years may it be called Riserva. Barbaresco: after four years it may be called Riserva.

CMS Certified column (Piedmont): top Barolo vineyards Cannubi, Brunate, Monprivato; top Barbaresco vineyards Ovello, Montestefano, Pora, Asili; Asti DOCG fully sparkling Moscato; Alta Langa DOCG metodo classico, min 90% Pinot Noir and/or Chardonnay; Roero DOCG Nebbiolo; Roero Arneis DOCG; Ghemme and Gattinara DOCG Nebbiolo, locally Spanna.

CMS Certified column (Piedmont): label terms normale, riserva; sorì = best (privileged) site; producers Barolo - Vietti, Giacomo Conterno, Bruno Giacosa, Ceretto, Sandrone, Elio Altare, Giuseppe Mascarello; Barbaresco - Gaja, La Spinetta, Produttori del Barbaresco; traditional vs modernist styles; long ageability; big tannins require meat or fat.

CMS Certified column (Lombardy/Emilia-Romagna): Valtellina Superiore DOCG dry red Nebbiolo, locally Chiavennasca; Sforzato di Valtellina DOCG passito-dried Chiavennasca; Franciacorta Satèn DOCG Brut only, max 5 atmospheres, Chardonnay with up to 50% Pinot Bianco; Lambrusco DOC frizzante or spumante, subzones Lambrusco di Sorbara, Grasparossa di Castelvetro, Salamino di Santa Croce; sweetness secco, amabile, dolce; producers Bellavista, Ca' del Bosco; Lambrusco has limited shelf life by the glass.
Franciacorta regulations: minimum time on lees Franciacorta 18 months; Satèn 24; Rosé 24; Millesimato 30; Riserva 60.

CMS Certified column (Veneto): Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG; Recioto di Soave DOCG sweet Garganega, appassimento; Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG sweet red, Corvina and Rondinella; Valpolicella Ripasso DOC uses the remaining must and lees from Recioto and/or Amarone, a short second fermentation giving more flavor, tannin and alcohol. Producers: Bertani, Masi, Allegrini, Quintarelli, Dal Forno; Friuli: Jermann, Livio Felluga, Josko Gravner; Alto Adige: Cantina Terlano, Tiefenbrunner; many Alto Adige producers are co-ops.
Valpolicella consortium: the four wines are Valpolicella DOC, Valpolicella Ripasso DOC, Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG and Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG.

CMS Certified column (Tuscany): Montalcino soils - clay and marine sediments at lower elevation, galestro at higher elevation; red grapes add Prugnolo Gentile, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc; whites Trebbiano, Vermentino, Vernaccia; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG, Bolgheri DOC, Rosso di Montepulciano DOC, Vin Santo DOCs; Gran Selezione exists.
Brunello di Montalcino DOCG is Sangiovese ('Brunello' in Montalcino); 2 years in oak and 4 months in bottle (6 for Riserva).
Chianti Classico: Annata min 80% Sangiovese; Gran Selezione min 90% Sangiovese, estate grapes only, min 30 months.
CMS curriculum: Chianti min 70% Sangiovese; Chianti Classico min 80%; Brunello 100%.
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano: min 70% Sangiovese from the commune of Montepulciano; the consortium writes 'Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile)'.

CMS Certified column (Tuscany): Super Tuscan can be Bordeaux grape blends, Bordeaux varieties with Sangiovese, or pure Sangiovese; producers Antinori, Ruffino, Sassicaia, Ornellaia, Masseto, Tignanello, Solaia, Biondi Santi, Banfi, Soldera; decant young Brunello; know top Brunello vintages and current release.

CMS Certified column (Central & Southern Italy): Marche - Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC, Verdicchio di Matelica DOC; Umbria - Sagrantino di Montefalco DOCG; Abruzzo - Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC; Campania - Taurasi DOCG, Greco di Tufo DOCG, Fiano di Avellino DOCG; volcanic soils in Campania; young Taurasi and Sagrantino di Montefalco should be decanted.
Bolgheri reds may use Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc (0-100%), Syrah and Sangiovese up to 50%.
Federdoc, Campania: Taurasi DOCG Aglianico min 85%; Fiano di Avellino DOCG Fiano min 85%; Greco di Tufo DOCG Greco min 85%.

CMS Certified column (Sicily & Sardinia): Etna DOC (Rosso and Bianco); Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG; Marsala DOC (Secco, Semi-Secco, Dolce); Sicilian whites Grillo, Inzolia, Catarratto; Cannonau di Sardegna DOC; Vermentino di Sardegna DOC; volcanic soil on Etna.
Federdoc, Sicily: Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG Nero d'Avola 50-70%, Frappato 30-50%; Etna DOC white Carricante 60-80%, red Nerello Mascalese min 80%.
Federdoc, Sardinia: Vermentino di Gallura DOCG min 95% Vermentino; Cannonau di Sardegna DOC min 85% Cannonau.

CMS Certified column (Rioja): subzones Rioja Alta, Rioja Oriental, Rioja Alavesa; Alta is continental, Alavesa the coolest and wettest, Oriental Mediterranean; soils calcareous clay, ferrous clay, alluvial; grapes add Garnacha, Mazuelo, Graciano, Malvasia, Garnacha Blanca; carbonic maceration common on Joven; Viñedo Singular.
CMS Certified column (Rioja tinto aging): Crianza min 2 years incl. 1 in oak; Reserva min 3 years incl. 1 in oak; Gran Reserva min 5 years incl. 2 in oak.
Rioja: Gran Reserva = minimum 5 years, 2 in barrel plus 2 in bottle; Reserva = minimum 3 years, at least 1 in barrel.

CMS Certified column (Rioja): some modern producers make fruit-focused wines with French oak and avoid Crianza/Reserva/Gran Reserva terms; Gran Reserva typically made only in the best vintages; Bordeaux and Rioja relationship during phylloxera; producers Marqués de Riscal, Marqués de Cáceres, Finca Allende, López de Heredia, La Rioja Alta.

CMS Certified column (Castilla y León): Tempranillo synonyms Tinta del País, Tinta de Toro; Bierzo DO Mencía; Ribera del Duero Crianza/Reserva/Gran Reserva as Rioja; producers Vega Sicilia, Pesquera, Pingus; Bierzo Descendientes de J. Palacios; Rueda Martinsancho; Rueda fresh whites from Verdejo and Sauvignon Blanc; Toro ripe, concentrated Tempranillo.
CMS Certified (Galicia): Valdeorras DO Godello whites and Mencía reds; Ribeira Sacra DO steep terraced slopes, Mencía, Godello, Albariño; producers Pazo Señorans, Granbazán, Lagar de Cervera.

CMS Certified column (Catalonia): Priorat bush vine (gobelet) training, no mechanization, llicorella soil, significant diurnal shifts; Gratallops project; producers René Barbier (Clos Mogador), Álvaro Palacios, Clos Erasmus, Clos Martinet, Scala Dei; Cava covers all of Spain but most is made in Penedès; Cava de Guarda min 9 months on lees, Reserva min 18; gyropalette a Spanish invention; Cava producer Gramona.
Cava aging: Cava de Guarda minimum 9 months; Reserva over 18 months; Gran Reserva 30 months; Cava de Paraje Calificado over 36 months.

CMS Certified (Spain Other DOs): País Vasco - Bizkaiko, Getariako and Arabako Txakolina DOs, primarily dry white, lightly effervescent, high acidity, early drinking, Hondarrabi Zuri (white) and Hondarrabi Beltza (red); Murcia - Jumilla DO, Monastrell, historically ungrafted vines due to sandy soil, avoided phylloxera until the 1980s, producer Juan Gil; DO Pago - created 2003, 20 as of 2022, producer appellations; Txakoli with oily seafood.

CMS Certified column (Portugal): Douro subregions Cima Corgo, Baixo Corgo, Douro Superior; Dão, Alentejo and Bairrada DOPs; terraces on the mountainsides; label term Single Quinta; lagares = stone fermenters; Madeira grapes Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey, Tinta Negra; Touriga Nacional for Douro and Porto.
Dão: surrounded by mountains, poor granite soils, vineyards from 200 to 1,000 m; Encruzado white; Touriga Nacional red.

CMS Certified column (Germany): Nahe - Nahe River a Rhine tributary, Riesling; Franken - along the Main near Frankfurt, Silvaner, Spätburgunder, Bocksbeutel bottle; Baden - along French and Swiss borders, warmest growing area, Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau; Mittelrhein - steep slopes on the Rhine, Riesling, slate; Ahr - one of the smallest and most northerly regions, north of the 50th parallel, Spätburgunder (some of Germany's best).

CMS Certified column (Germany): VDP national association with its own Burgundy-model classification; Grosses Gewächs = single vineyard grand cru wines; Erstes Gewächs = premier cru; general terms Gemeinde (village), Einzellage (single vineyard), Oechsle scale for must weight, Bocksbeutel; label terms Halbtrocken half-dry, Edelfäule noble rot, Schloss castle; Deutscher Sekt sparkling from German grapes; extra grapes Müller-Thurgau, Silvaner, Weissburgunder, Grauburgunder.
VDP: dry wines from Grosse Lage vineyards are called VDP.Grosses Gewächs; it is the VDP's private rule, not German wine law.

CMS Certified column (Germany): 1971 German Wine Law made ripeness at harvest the prime determinant of quality; know where each style belongs on a wine list and serving temperatures; producers Dönnhoff (Nahe), Hans Wirsching (Franken), Künstler, Robert Weil, Leitz (Rheingau), Gunderloch (Rheinhessen), Fritz Haag, Dr. Loosen, Egon Müller, J.J. Prüm, Selbach-Oster (Mosel).

CMS Certified column (Austria): Kremstal DAC along the Krems River, Kamptal DAC along the Kamp, both dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling; Wachau classification Steinfeder, Federspiel, Smaragd; Banderole = Austrian capsule marking Qualitätswein or higher; regions Burgenland (Mittelburgenland), Steiermark, Wien; producers Emmerich Knoll, Rudi Pichler, FX Pichler, Prager, Schloss Gobelsburg, Bründlmayer; Grüner pairs with seafood, vegetables, herbs, asparagus and artichokes.
Vinea Wachau: all white, dry, no oak. Steinfeder up to 11.5% alcohol (feather grass); Federspiel not more than 12.5% (falconry); Smaragd at least 12.5% (emerald-green lizard).

CMS Certified column (Hungary): Bodrog River creates humidity in Tokaj; puttonyos = the basket aszú grapes were gathered in; aszú = shriveled, botrytis-affected berries; grapes Furmint and Hárslevelű; Eszencia made entirely of aszú berries; producer Royal Tokaji; Tokaji not made during the communist years 1949-1989; pair with foie gras, blue cheese, orchard tarts; bottles normally 500 ml.
In Tokaj, since 2013, 120 g/l is the minimum residual sugar for Aszú (equivalent to the old 5 puttony); Aszú must age at least 18 months in wooden casks.

CMS Certified (Greece): Santorini PDO - warm Mediterranean, Aegean salt air, volcanic, basket-shaped vines against wind, Assyrtiko, producer Sigalas; Naoussa PDO - continental, Xinomavro; Nemea PDO - Agiorgitiko. Assyrtiko pairs with seafood, roasted fish and fresh cheeses; Xinomavro needs lamb or beef to tame the tannins.

PDO Santorini (est. 1971): volcanic soils, self-rooted vines never affected by phylloxera; basket-trained 'kouloura' vines protect against strong winds; dry wines at least 85% Assyrtiko with Athiri and Aidani; 'Nykteri' = dry, at least 13.5% and 3 months in oak; 'Vinsanto' = sweet wine from sun-dried grapes.
PDO Naoussa: on the south-eastern slopes of Mt Vermio, temperate Mediterranean climate with continental influences; exclusively red wines from 100% Xinomavro; pale color, high tannins, high acidity.

PDO Nemea: in Korinthia (and a small part of Argolida); Greece's largest PDO zone for red wines, from about 230 to 850 m; exclusively red wines from 100% Agiorgitiko; red fruit, sweet spice, velvety texture.
The PDO Santorini wine production zone was established in 1971.
The PDO Naoussa wine production zone was established in 1971.
The PDO Nemea wine production zone was established in 1971.
Barbaresco: 100% Nebbiolo; ages at least two years, nine months in oak; after four years it may be called Riserva.
Alsace Grand Cru: Riesling, Muscat, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer are the traditional Grand Cru grapes.

court.outcome:
FRANCE - BORDEAUX: After studying this section, a candidate will be able to connect grape variety, geography, soil type, and wine style with important Bordeaux appellations. They will be able to identify key regions on map, distinguish the unique aspects of the different regions of Bordeaux in regional classification systems, vintages, and styles of wine produced. A candidate will understand the impact of these differences when making purchasing decisions and when making recommendations. Certified Sommeliers will recognize iconic producers and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with the various styles of wine from Bordeaux to a guest.

FRANCE - BURGUNDY: After studying this section, a candidate will be able to identify major villages, grand crus, soil types, and winemaking styles for each area of Burgundy. A Certified Sommeliers will recognize iconic producers and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with the various wines from Burgundy to a guest.

FRANCE - LOIRE VALLEY: After studying this section, a candidate will know the major regions and selected appellations of the Loire Valley and be able to connect the grape varieties to their appellations. Candidates will be able to recommend and sell food pairings with Loire Valley wines. Certified Sommeliers will recognize iconic producers and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with wines from the Loire Valley to a guest.

FRANCE - THE RHÔNE VALLEY: After studying this section, a candidate will be able to identify the primary and secondary AOCs and Crus, know their locations, primary grape varieties, and general style. Candidates will understand and connect differences in quality and price among AOPs/Crus to physical features and landscape. Certified Sommeliers will recognize iconic producers and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with wines from the Rhône Valley to a guest.

FRANCE - ALSACE: After studying this section, a candidate will understand the classification of Alsatian wine and be able to identify important Grands Crus vineyard names. A Certified Sommelier will be able to recognize iconic producers and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with wines from Alsace to a guest.

FRANCE - SOUTH FRANCE: After studying this section, a candidate will be able to match regions in the South of France with their grape varieties and styles of wine made.

ITALY - NORTHERN ITALY - PIEDMONT: After studying this section, a candidate will know the major DOCGs within Piedmont, know their grape varieties, understand their styles, aging requirements, and labeling laws. A Certified Sommelier will be able to recognize iconic producers and be able to sell and recommend food pairings with Barolo and Barbaresco to a guest.

ITALY - NORTHERN ITALY - LOMBARDY & EMILIA-ROMAGNA: After studying this section, a student will be able to understand different styles of Franciacorta, know the grape variety and style of Valtellina Superiore DOCG, and know the styles and sub-zones of Lambrusco. A Certified Sommelier recognize iconic producers and be able to sell and recommend food pairings with Franciacorta to a guest.

ITALY - NORTHERN ITALY - TRENTINO-ALTO ADIGE / FRIULI / VENETO: After studying this section, a candidate will know a broader range of DOC/DOCGs in Northeast Italy, match grape varieties to their regions, and understand winemaking styles. A Certified Sommelier will be able to recognize iconic producers and be able to sell and recommend food pairings with wines from these regions to a guest.

ITALY - TUSCANY: After studying this section, a candidate will understand the differences between multiple regions of Sangiovese, and know and understand DOC/DOCG wines from regions in Tuscany. A Certified Sommelier recognize iconic producers and be able to sell and recommend food pairings with wines from Tuscany to a guest.

ITALY - CENTRAL & SOUTHERN ITALY: After studying this section, a candidate will know the DOC/DOCGs in Central and Southern Italy, match grape varieties to their regions, and understand winemaking styles.

ITALY - ISLANDS - SICILY & SARDINIA: After studying this section, a candidate will be able to match grape varieties to major DOC/DOCGs and know the larger region within Italy in which they are located.

SPAIN - GALICIA: After studying this section, a candidate will know the soil type and the styles and grape varieties of Valdeorras DO and Ribeira Sacra DO.  A Certified Sommelier will be able to recognize iconic producers and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with Rías Baixas Albariño to a guest.

SPAIN - LA RIOJA: After studying this section, a candidate will have a deeper knowledge of Rioja, including the subzones, specific aging requirements, iconic producers, and differences between traditional and modern styles. A Certified Sommelier will be able to recognize iconic producers and be able to sell and recommend food pairings with wines from Rioja to a guest.

SPAIN - CASTILLA Y LEÓN: After studying this section, a candidate will have deeper knowledge of the major DOs within Castilla y León, including specific aging requirements. A Certified Sommelier will be able to recognize iconic producers and be able to sell and recommend food pairings with wines from Ribera del Duero to a guest.

SPAIN - CATALONIA / CATALUNYA: After studying this section, a candidate will have a deeper understanding of Priorat DOCa and Cava DO, including aging requirements. A Certified Sommelier will be able to recognize iconic producers and be able to sell and recommend food pairings with wines from these regions to a guest.

SPAIN - OTHER DOs: After studying this section, a student will know the  styles of wine made in selected DOs beyond the classic regions.

PORTUGAL: After studying this section, a candidate will be able to match major grape varieties to their respective DOPs and styles. Certified Sommeliers will be able to recommend and sell food pairings with wines from Portugal to a guest.

GERMANY: After studying this section, a candidate will expand their knowledge of wine terms, label terms, history, lore, and classifications. A candidate will be able to describe the general styles of finished wine, including structure and flavors. A Certified Sommelier will know the proper ways to include the wines of Germany on a wine list, be able to recognize iconic producers, and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with these wines to a guest.

AUSTRIA: After studying this section, a candidate will increase their knowledge of general terms, styles of wine, and classifications in Austria. A Certified Sommelier will be able to recognize iconic producers and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with Austrian Grüner Veltliner to a guest.

HUNGARY: After studying this section, a student will understand Tokaji's grape growing and winemaking. A Certified Sommelier will be able to sell and recommend food pairings with Tokaji to a guest.

GREECE: After studying this section, a candidate will know the location, climate, and grape varieties of three important wine regions of Greece. Certified Sommeliers will recognize iconic producers and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with wines from Greece to a guest.

read.bigIdea: Certified means every village and Grand Cru.
read.where: From Level 1: Burgundy runs from **Chablis** south to **Beaujolais**, with four levels from Régionale up to **Grand Cru**. Now learn the names inside each level. The Court expects every Côte d’Or village and its Grands Crus, all seven **Chablis** Grands Crus and all ten **Beaujolais** crus.

stops.name: Chablis
stops.text: **Petit Chablis** grows on harder **Portlandian** limestone; Chablis and its crus on **Kimmeridgian** limestone and marl. Top growers: **Dauvissat** and **Raveneau**.

stops.name: Côte de Nuits
stops.text: The heart of the Grands Crus, mainly Pinot Noir: **Chambertin**, **Clos de Vougeot**, **Musigny**, **Romanée-Conti**, **La Tâche** and more. There is also a **Côte de Nuits-Villages** appellation.

stops.name: Côte de Beaune
stops.text: Reds around Beaune (**Volnay**, **Pommard**); Chardonnay from **Meursault** south. Grands Crus include **Corton-Charlemagne** and five Montrachets.

stops.name: Chalonnaise and Mâconnais
stops.text: **Bouzeron** (100% Aligoté), **Rully**, **Mercurey**, **Givry**, **Montagny**. In the Mâconnais, **Pouilly-Fuissé** has Premier Cru vineyards.

stops.name: Beaujolais
stops.text: Ten crus, including **Fleurie**, **Moulin-à-Vent** and **Morgon**. Morgon is the largest; its **Côte du Py** is decomposed shale.

read.visualIntro: Two lists to learn by heart:
read.mixup: **Jadot**, **Latour** and **Drouhin** are large **négociants**. **DRC**, **Leroy** and **Leflaive** are the Court’s top Côte d’Or **domaines**.
read.sayIt: This is a Côte de Nuits Grand Cru: Pinot Noir from one of Burgundy’s top vineyards.

read.bigIdea: Two white-wine regions, now soil by soil.
read.where: From Level 1: the Loire runs from the Atlantic to central France, and Alsace hides behind the Vosges. Certified adds **soils**, **sweetness words** and **producers** for both. It also splits Alsace into **Bas-Rhin** and **Haut-Rhin**.

stops.name: Loire soils
stops.text: **Tuffeau** limestone under Vouvray, plus **silex** (flint) and **Kimmeridgian** clay. Humidity from the **Layon River** brings botrytis to Quarts de Chaume and Bonnezeaux.

stops.name: Alsace, north and south

stops.name: Alsace in the cellar
stops.text: Large neutral **foudres**, little new oak. More grapes: **Pinot Blanc**, **Sylvaner**, **Chardonnay**, **Auxerrois**. Every Alsace AOP wine goes in the traditional **Flûte d’Alsace** bottle.

read.mixup: **Edelzwicker** and **Gentil** are both Alsace blends. A grape name on the label means **100%** that grape.
read.sayIt: A Crémant d’Alsace: traditional-method bubbles at a friendlier price.

read.where: From Level 1: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva climb in time. Certified gives the **actual years**, Rioja’s **subzones**, more DOs and Portugal’s **DOPs**.

stops.name: Rioja
stops.text: **Alta**, **Alavesa**, **Oriental**. Joven is often carbonic; some modern wines use French oak and skip the aging words. Names: **López de Heredia**, **La Rioja Alta**, **Marqués de Riscal**.

stops.name: Castilla y León
stops.text: **Ribera del Duero** (Vega Sicilia, Pesquera, Pingus) uses Rioja’s ladder. **Toro** is ripe Tinta de Toro; **Bierzo** is Mencía; **Rueda** is Verdejo.

stops.name: Galicia and Catalonia
stops.text: **Valdeorras** (Godello) and terraced **Ribeira Sacra** (Mencía). **Priorat** grows bush vines on **llicorella**. **Cava** needs 9 months on lees, Reserva 18.

stops.name: Other DOs
stops.text: Basque **Txakolina** (Hondarrabi Zuri), **Jumilla** (Monastrell, once ungrafted), and **Vino de Pago**, producer appellations created in 2003.

stops.name: Portugal

stops.name: More Anbaugebiete

stops.name: Label words
stops.text: **Einzellage** is a single vineyard, **Gemeinde** a village, **Halbtrocken** half-dry, **Edelfäule** noble rot, **Schloss** a castle. **Oechsle** measures must weight.

stops.name: The VDP
stops.text: Its own Burgundy-style ranking: **Grosses Gewächs** is the dry grand cru, **Erstes Gewächs** the premier cru. Names: **Dönnhoff**, **Robert Weil**, **Egon Müller**, **J.J. Prüm**.

stops.name: Austria
stops.text: **Kremstal** and **Kamptal** DACs for dry Grüner and Riesling; the Wachau’s **Steinfeder**, **Federspiel**, **Smaragd**. Names: **FX Pichler**, **Knoll**, **Prager**, **Bründlmayer**.

read.mixup: **Grosses Gewächs** is the VDP’s dry grand cru. **Erstes Gewächs** is its premier cru.
read.sayIt: A Grüner Veltliner: crisp and dry, and great with asparagus.

read.bigIdea: One great sweet wine, three Greek classics.
read.where: From Level 1: **Tokaji** is Hungary’s noble-rot wine. Certified adds how it’s grown and made. It also adds three Greek **PDOs**, each with its own grape.

stops.name: Tokaj
stops.text: The **Bodrog River** brings humidity. Botrytis shrivels **Furmint** and **Hárslevelű** into **aszú** berries, once gathered in a basket called a **puttony**.

stops.name: Tokaji on the label
stops.text: **Aszú** needs at least **120 g/L** of sugar and 18 months in cask. **Eszencia** is pure aszú. Bottles are usually **500 ml**; **Royal Tokaji** is a name to know.

stops.name: Santorini
stops.text: Ungrafted vines trained as low **baskets** on volcanic soil. Dry Santorini is at least **85% Assyrtiko**. **Sigalas** is the Court’s producer.

stops.name: Naoussa and Nemea
stops.text: **Naoussa**, on Mt Vermio, is 100% **Xinomavro**: pale, tannic, high in acid. **Nemea**, in Korinthia, is 100% **Agiorgitiko**: red fruit and a velvety texture.

read.mixup: **Nykteri** is an oak-aged dry Santorini. **Vinsanto** is Santorini’s sweet wine from sun-dried grapes.
read.sayIt: Santorini Assyrtiko: bright and salty, perfect with grilled fish.
